q: מטופל בגיר מאושפז זקוק לטיפול רפואי דחוף ואינו מסוגל לתת הסכמה מדעת. אין לו אפוטרופוס, ייפוי כוח תקף או הנחיות מקדימות ידועות. אין בן זוג, ילדים או הורים, ושני אחיו מסכימים מי מהם ייצג אותו. לאחר הליך האישור במוסד, מי מהבאים יכול לשמש מקבל החלטות זמני?
o: הרופא המומחה שקבע את הדחיפות ואת אי־היכולת להסכים
האח הבגיר שנבחר בהסכמה לשמש כנציגו של המטופל
העובד הסוציאלי המרכז את בירור ההסכמה בין קרוביו
מנהל המוסד הרפואי הבוחן את הבקשה לאישור הנציג
explanation:
**מקבל החלטות זמני** הוא נציג משפחתי המאושר בהליך מוגדר עבור טיפול רפואי דחוף כשמטופל בגיר אינו מסוגל להסכים ואין נציג רפואי קיים. הרופא קובע את הצורך ואת אי־היכולת להסכים, העובד הסוציאלי מברר את ההסכמה המשפחתית, ומנהל המוסד או המוסמך מטעמו מאשר את המינוי. התפקידים המקצועיים הללו מובחנים מתפקיד בן המשפחה המקבל את ההחלטות (נוהל מקבל החלטות זמני, עמ׳ 1, 2).
"ובכך יכנס האישור לתוקף ואותו בן משפחה יהיה מוסמך לקבל החלטות בעניין הטיפול במטופל." (עמ׳ 2).

**א. הרופא המומחה שקבע את הדחיפות ואת אי־היכולת להסכים.** שגויה, הרופא המומחה קובע את הצורך הרפואי ואת אי־היכולת להסכים. תפקיד קביעה זה אינו המינוי לנציג משפחתי שמקבל החלטות עבור המטופל (עמ׳ 1, 2).
**ב. האח הבגיר שנבחר בהסכמה לשמש כנציגו של המטופל.** נכונה, האח נמצא במדרג המשפחתי המתואר, קיימת הסכמת האחים, ובשאלה הושלם הליך האישור. עם כניסת האישור לתוקף בן המשפחה מוסמך לקבל החלטות בעניין הטיפול (עמ׳ 2).
**ג. העובד הסוציאלי המרכז את בירור ההסכמה בין קרוביו.** שגויה, העובד הסוציאלי מברר את ההסכמה המשפחתית ומחתים את הנציג שנבחר. הוא אינו הופך מכוח תפקידו לנציג המשפחה (עמ׳ 2).
**ד. מנהל המוסד הרפואי הבוחן את הבקשה לאישור הנציג.** שגויה, מנהל המוסד בוחן ומאשר את הבקשה. האישור מעניק סמכות לבן המשפחה שנבחר, ולא למנהל שבדק את הבקשה (עמ׳ 2).

מקור: משרד הבריאות, מקבל החלטות זמני לעניינים רפואיים, 15.02.2024, עמ׳ 1, 2, סעיפים 1 עד 4ז.
ref: מקבל החלטות זמני לעניינים רפואיים · PDF p. 2, section 4(d–g)

q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment has urgency incontinence. His family wishes to avoid an antimuscarinic drug. His postvoid residual is 180 mL and blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. Which listed bladder relaxant acts through beta-3 receptors?
o: Oxybutynin
Mirabegron
Tolterodine
Solifenacin
explanation:
**Beta-3 agonists** provide a different mechanism from antimuscarinic bladder relaxants (Table 47-12, p. 712). They still require attention to blood pressure and bladder emptying: "Bladder relaxants may rarely precipitate urinary retention in some patients" (p. 714).

**A. Oxybutynin.** Wrong, oxybutynin is listed among antimuscarinic agents, so it does not meet the requested mechanism (p. 712).
**B. Mirabegron.** Correct, mirabegron is listed as a beta-3 agonist, matching the requested non-antimuscarinic mechanism (pp. 712–714).
**C. Tolterodine.** Wrong, tolterodine is listed among antimuscarinic agents, retaining the mechanism the family wishes to avoid (p. 712).
**D. Solifenacin.** Wrong, solifenacin is listed among antimuscarinic agents, rather than beta-3 agonists (p. 712).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 712, 714.

q: An 80-year-old woman with moderate vascular dementia in a memory-care unit has refused bathing for two weeks and smells of urine. She becomes aggressive when approached with bathing equipment, but there is no immediate danger. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis and takes amlodipine 5 mg daily and acetaminophen 650 mg twice daily. Her daughter says she used to be meticulous about cleanliness. Alongside assessing causes of distress, which approach follows first-line behavioral care?
o: Start risperidone before attempting to adjust the bathing routine
Use a sedative before attempting to adjust the bathing routine
Try bathing at a calmer time using a reassuring approach
Increase bedtime medication before attempting to adjust the bathing routine
explanation:
**Nonpharmacologic care** is first-line for neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia unless immediate safety requires another approach. A calm, individualized interaction is consistent with that principle; choosing a calmer bathing time is an application to this trigger (pp. 925–926). "Nonpharmacologic interventions are first-line in the management of NPS in dementia patients to avoid the risks and side effects associated with medications." (p. 925).

**A. Start risperidone before attempting to adjust the bathing routine.** Wrong, behavioral approaches precede psychotropics outside specified urgent circumstances; no trial of such approaches is described (p. 925).
**B. Use a sedative before attempting to adjust the bathing routine.** Wrong, using sedation before adapting care bypasses the recommended first-line approach and adds medication risks (p. 925).
**C. Try bathing at a calmer time using a reassuring approach.** Correct, adapting the interaction and using a reassuring manner applies the nonpharmacologic guidance to bathing-related distress (pp. 925–926; inference about timing).
**D. Increase bedtime medication before attempting to adjust the bathing routine.** Wrong, escalating sleep medication does not implement the first-line behavioral adjustment to the bathing trigger (p. 925).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 925, 926.
ref: Hazzard Ch 60 — BEHAVIORAL SYMPTOMS OF DEMENTIA AND PSYCHOACTIVE DRUG THERAPY
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: An 81-year-old woman with dementia taking mirtazapine reports daytime sleepiness. Dose reduction is being considered to reduce sedation. Which information from Hazzard is relevant?
o: Lower doses may increase alertness and reduce daytime sleepiness
Lower doses may remain sedating and leave daytime sleepiness
Lower doses may improve sleep as shown by the described trial
Lower doses may reduce sleepiness as shown by the described trial
explanation:
**Mirtazapine** can be sedating at lower doses. The trial described in patients with dementia and sleep disturbance found no sleep benefit over placebo and increased daytime sleepiness, so lower dosing should not be presented as a demonstrated way to eliminate sedation (p. 930). "Mirtazapine can be sedating at lower doses and is sometimes used as a sleep aid." (p. 930).

**A. Lower doses may increase alertness and reduce daytime sleepiness.** Wrong, the low-dose effect described is sedation, not increased alertness (p. 930).
**B. Lower doses may remain sedating and leave daytime sleepiness.** Correct, sedation at lower doses is explicitly described, so daytime sleepiness can remain a concern (p. 930).
**C. Lower doses may improve sleep as shown by the described trial.** Wrong, the cited trial did not show improvement in sleep over placebo (p. 930).
**D. Lower doses may reduce sleepiness as shown by the described trial.** Wrong, the treated group experienced increased, rather than decreased, daytime sleepiness (p. 930).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 930.
ref: Hazzard Ch 60 — BEHAVIORAL SYMPTOMS OF DEMENTIA AND PSYCHOACTIVE DRUG THERAPY
chapterTitle: Behavioral Symptoms of Dementia and Psychoactive Drug Therapy

q: An 81-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 28% predicted) has been hospitalized three times in six months, lost 20 pounds, and now needs help bathing and dressing. He asks how much time he has left. His daughter interrupts, saying everything will be fine. Which response follows the communication approach described in Hazzard?
o: Acknowledge the difficulty, then provide a fixed survival estimate before exploring preferences
Acknowledge the difficulty, then redirect the discussion to comfort without exploring prognosis
Acknowledge the difficulty, then ask the patient how much prognostic information he wants
Acknowledge the difficulty, then follow the daughter’s preference for avoiding the prognosis
explanation:
**Information preferences and emotions** should be addressed during serious-illness conversations. Hazzard recommends clarifying what the patient wants to know, responding to emotional cues, and redirecting the conversation to the patient when a caregiver talks over them (pp. 1090–1093).
"Next, the patient’s preferences for information and medical decision making should be clarified." (p. 1090).
"Responding to emotional cues is a key aspect of successful communication, building trust, and supporting patients." (p. 1091).

**A. Acknowledge the difficulty, then provide a fixed survival estimate before exploring preferences.** Wrong, the recommended process clarifies the patient’s information preferences first; the supplied facts also do not establish a fixed survival estimate (p. 1090).
**B. Acknowledge the difficulty, then redirect the discussion to comfort without exploring prognosis.** Wrong, redirecting away from prognosis bypasses the patient’s question and the recommended clarification of information preferences (p. 1090).
**C. Acknowledge the difficulty, then ask the patient how much prognostic information he wants.** Correct, this combines an empathic response with clarification of the patient’s own information preferences (pp. 1090–1091).
**D. Acknowledge the difficulty, then follow the daughter’s preference for avoiding the prognosis.** Wrong, the source advises returning the conversation to the patient rather than letting a caregiver’s interruption determine its content (p. 1093).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1090, 1091, 1093.
ref: Hazzard Ch 71 — EFFECTIVE COMMUNICATION STRATEGIES FOR PATIENTS WITH SERIOUS ILLNESS
chapterTitle: Effective Communication Strategies For Patients with Serious Illness

q: A patient with COPD develops respiratory depression after an opioid overdose. Alongside respiratory support, treatment is needed to reverse the opioid effect. What is the role of naloxone here?
o: Reversal of the opioid effect during an overdose
Long-term medication treatment of opioid use disorder
Enhancement of the opioid effect for pain relief
Replacement of the opioid for continuing pain treatment
explanation:
**Naloxone** has a role in overdose reversal distinct from ongoing treatment of opioid use disorder (p. 326). "Naloxone does not treat OUD, but it can reverse potentially fatal opioid overdoses" (p. 326). That distinction matches the immediate need to reverse overdose in the stem.

**A. Reversal of the opioid effect during an overdose.** Correct, reversal of potentially fatal overdose is the role explicitly described and matches the acute problem (p. 326).
**B. Long-term medication treatment of opioid use disorder.** Wrong, the source expressly states that naloxone does not treat opioid use disorder (p. 326).
**C. Enhancement of the opioid effect for pain relief.** Wrong, enhancing opioid action would oppose the reversal role described for naloxone in this overdose (p. 326; application).
**D. Replacement of the opioid for continuing pain treatment.** Wrong, the source describes reversal of overdose, not substitution for ongoing opioid analgesia (p. 326; application).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 326.
ref: Hazzard Ch 23 — SUBSTANCE USE AND DISORDERS

q: במרפאה קרדיולוגית מעוניינים להכניס בדיקה לאבחון שבריריות שתתבצע לפני החלטה על פרוצדורת החלפת מסתם אאורטלי בצינתור Transcatheter Aortic-Valve Implantation (TAVI). מה ההמלצה המתאימה בהתייחס למדדי שבריריות שונים?
o: מדד FRIED ניתן לבצע בתשאול טלפוני
ניתן לבצע מדד Deficit Accumulation Index or Frailty Index (FI) אחרי הערכה כוללנית של גריאטר בקהילה
במידה ורוצים להשתמש באבחון שבריריות מתוך תיק רפואי מומלץ להשתמש במדד Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) של Rockwood
מדד FRAIL מחייב בדיקה גופנית במרפאה
explanation:
Official answer: ב

The **Frailty Index (FI)** uses accumulated deficits from comprehensive geriatric assessment. Choice of measure depends on available information and the need for direct physical measurement (pp. 620–623).

**A. Fried’s measure can be completed by telephone.** Wrong, grip-strength and gait-speed measurements cannot be supplied by telephone interview alone (pp. 620–622).
**B. Calculate a Deficit Accumulation Index or FI after community geriatric assessment.** Correct, medical, functional and cognitive deficits documented in comprehensive assessment can supply the index (pp. 622–623).
**C. Use Rockwood’s Clinical Frailty Scale for assessment from medical records.** Wrong, not accepted for scoring. The source describes an overall clinical judgment but does not prohibit record information; distinguish the key from the limit of source support (p. 623).
**D. FRAIL requires a physical examination in clinic.** Wrong, FRAIL uses reported information, so physical examination is not intrinsically required (pp. 622–623).

Rockwood’s CFS is based on the clinician’s overall impression; the source does not impose a blanket prohibition on information from medical records (p. 623).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 620, 621, 622, 623.
referenceNote: Printed IMA citation retained; checked explanation source: Hazzard 8e · p. 620-623.

q: A person has low muscle mass, preserved gait/grip, and low food intake without a catabolic disease. Which diagnosis does this chapter prioritize?
o: Malnutrition
Physical frailty
Cachexia
Sarcopenia
explanation:
When low muscle mass is not accompanied by low muscle function, the chapter prioritizes malnutrition as the main diagnosis (p736).

D. Sarcopenia: Preserved grip and gait do not supply the low-function component; the chapter prioritizes malnutrition in this pattern (p736).
C. Cachexia: The chapter describes disease-associated wasting with excess catabolism and inflammation, absent from the stem (p736).
B. Physical frailty: The physical frailty construct includes weakness and slowness; isolated low mass with preserved function does not establish it (p736).

q: What core process causes MDS-associated cytopenias?
o: Ineffective clonal hematopoiesis with impaired maturation and differentiation
Destruction of red cells by CLL-associated autoantibodies
A stable diabetic nephropathy satisfying myeloma end-organ criteria
Effective hematopoiesis with unrestricted maturation of affected lineages
explanation:
MDS consists of clonal disorders with ineffective hematopoiesis and impaired maturation and differentiation, producing cytopenias (p1483).

D. Effective hematopoiesis with unrestricted maturation of affected lineages: Affected MDS lineages cannot undergo normal maturation and differentiation (p1483).
B. Destruction of red cells by CLL-associated autoantibodies: This is a CLL autoimmune mechanism, not the defining MDS process (p1492).
C. A stable diabetic nephropathy satisfying myeloma end-organ criteria: Stable diabetic nephropathy is a competing explanation, not myeloma-related damage or the MDS mechanism (p1503).
